body.objective: Students will be able to plan a fair test.
body.iCan: I can plan a fair test.
successCriteria: I can plan a fair test with one variable changed
I can choose what to measure and how
I can predict results before testing
body.hook: When engineers test a bridge design, they don't change the weight, the wind and the material all at once. If the bridge fails, they need to know exactly why. That is the idea behind a fair test.

vocabulary.definition: A test where only one thing is changed and everything else stays the same.
Anything that can change in a test.
The one thing you change on purpose.
What you measure to see the effect.
Things kept the same so the test is fair.
What you think will happen, with a reason.

study.title: Test Planner
study.question: How do I plan a test that gives trustworthy results?
study.passage:
Test planning sheet (written for this lesson):
Testing question: "Does the thickness of the base change how much weight my organizer can hold before it bends 5 mm?"
Independent variable: base thickness (3 mm, 6 mm, 9 mm card or wood).
Dependent variable: mass (in grams) added before the base bends 5 mm.
Controlled variables: same material, same base size, same supports, same way of adding mass (100 g at a time), same person measuring the bend.
Prediction: "I predict the 9 mm base will hold the most because thicker material is stiffer."
Repeat: Do each test three times and find the average.
Your task: Write a testing question for your own prototype. Choose one independent variable, one dependent variable and at least three controlled variables. Write a prediction with a reason.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Identify the independent, dependent and controlled variables
Write a testing question for your prototype
List variables and write a prediction
Plan how many times you will repeat the test
discussion: What would happen if two variables changed at once?
Is your prediction based on a reason?
study.product: Write a complete fair-test plan for one feature of your prototype.

body.objective: Students will be able to record and analyze results.

body.hook: Numbers on their own can hide the story. A table of 15 test results looks like noise; a simple bar graph can show the answer in one glance. Today you turn test data into evidence.

study.title: Data to Decision
study.question: What do my test results tell me about my design?
study.passage:
Sample results (written for this lesson), base-thickness test:
3 mm base: trial 1 = 400 g, trial 2 = 500 g, trial 3 = 450 g
6 mm base: trial 1 = 900 g, trial 2 = 1,000 g, trial 3 = 950 g
9 mm base: trial 1 = 1,500 g, trial 2 = 1,600 g, trial 3 = 600 g (the base slipped off a support)
Steps: 1. Calculate the average for each thickness. 2. Decide whether any result is an outlier and why. If an outlier was caused by an error, redo that trial or leave it out and say so. 3. Draw a bar graph: thickness on the x-axis, average mass on the y-axis, with a title and labels. 4. Write a conclusion: answer the testing question, use numbers, compare with your prediction.
Then do the same with your own test data.

body.objective: Students will be able to improve the design.
successCriteria: I can explain iteration and why failure helps design
I can use evidence to redesign my prototype
I can test whether my redesign is an improvement
body.hook: James Dyson built 5,127 prototypes of his bagless vacuum cleaner over about five years before one worked well enough to sell. Each "failure" taught him something. Iteration is the engine of good design.

vocabulary.definition: Repeating the cycle of design, test and improve.
To change a design based on evidence.
A result that does not meet the criteria, which gives information to improve.
Testing the old and new versions the same way to compare them.
The real reason a problem happens.

study.title: Iterate!
study.question: How does each iteration make my design better?
study.passage:
Iteration worksheet (written for this lesson):
1. Problem: Name one criterion your prototype did not meet, with evidence. Example: "The base bent 8 mm with 600 g of books; the criterion is less than 5 mm."
2. Root cause: Ask "Why?" until you reach the real reason. Why did it bend? The base is thin. Why is it thin? We used 3 mm card to save cost. Why? We didn't know the strength needed.
3. Redesign options: list two or three fixes (thicker base, add a support rib, change material).
4. Choose and justify one fix using your test data and cost.
5. Build the change.
6. Retest exactly as before and compare before and after.
7. Decide: Is it better? Does it now meet the criterion? Is another iteration needed?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; Dyson figure from his widely reported account.
steps: Identify a failed criterion with evidence
List and choose a redesign option
Build the change and retest the same way
Compare before and after and decide on the next iteration
discussion: What was the root cause of your problem?
Why did you choose that fix?
Did the redesign improve the result? By how much?
What would your next iteration be?
